svg.text: Oil + iron-oxide droplets grab microplastics, an electromagnet holds them in the chamber while clean water drains out, then the water is UV-treated and stored. The captured plastics can be lifted out and counted.
Shown in the "capture" state: coil on, dark ferrofluid spikes (with plastic specks) held at the bottom wall.
B · Section: how the water moves

g.text: jet spins the water to mix
oil droplets coat and grab plastics
pulled to the wall by the field
switch on to capture and hold
Dose and swirl. Tiny droplets of
repelling, so they stick to the oil
The field pulls the droplets, and
the plastics inside them, onto the
lower wall. The drain opens and
clean water flows down through the
filter disc into the UV tank.
Lift the glass chamber out. Rinse
the oil away, pull the magnetite
back out with a magnet, and collect

svg.text: Magnetite can be recovered and reused [1].
D · Using it, and what the evidence says

g.text: Oil must be food-grade. The best result in [1] used lubricating oil
(98 %), which is not safe for drinking water. Cooking oil still
removed over 95 % in the same tests; carbon then polishes out traces.
Evidence is strongest for big pieces. [1] tested 2 mm PET (up to
99 %) and got 64 % in real laundry wastewater. Coated iron particles
recovered about 92 % of 10–20 µm PE/PS from seawater [2].
The coil needs a battery. A sliding neodymium magnet ring could
replace it for a version with no electronics at all.
Dose used in [1]: about 0.5 mL oil and 0.25–1.25 g Fe₃O₄ per litre.
Removal was the same across that magnetite range.
Still to test: food-grade oil at drinking-water particle
sizes, and how much oil gets past the carbon.

[1] Hamzah, S. et al. (2021). Synthesis, characterisation and evaluation on the performance of ferrofluid for microplastic removal from synthetic and actual wastewater. J. Environ. Chem. Eng. 9, 105894.
[2] Grbic, J. et al. (2019). Magnetic extraction of microplastics from environmental samples. Environ. Sci. Technol. Lett. 6(2), 68–72.
